steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Many robotic applications need nearest neighbors search (NNS), for example real-time LiDAR-based simultaneous localization and mapping (SLAM) and motion planning, where data is sampled sequentially and real-time mapping is essential. In LiDAR-based SLAM, NNS is crucial for computing features, estimating normals, and matching new points to the map. Recent advances in LiDAR technology have reduced the cost, size, weight, and power of LiDAR significantly, and also made LiDAR high performance, so it has become an essential sensor for robots. But this also makes NNS more challenging. A current LiDAR sensor can produce a large amount of 3D points per second, with centimeter accuracy at a measuring range of hundreds of meters. This large amount of sequential data has to be processed in real-time, which is quite challenging on robots that have limited onboard computing resources. So to make NNS efficient, it is very important to maintain a large map that supports highly efficient queries and dynamic updates with newly arriving points in real-time.

Various static tree data structures have been proposed, but they struggle to meet these demands. R-tree and R \ast -tree partition the data by grouping nearby points into their minimum bounding rectangle in the next higher level of the tree. k-d tree is a well-known instance of splitting the space. The octree splits the space recursively into eight equal axis-aligned cubes, and these form the volumes represented by eight child nodes. k-d tree is a favored data structure in general k-nearest neighbors (KNN) search libraries, but it is hard to draw a final conclusion on whether the k-d tree is better suited for NNS than other data structures. Comparative studies show that different implementations of k-d trees can perform very differently, and that the octree is among the best performing algorithms, especially for radius search, because it partitions the search space regularly. Even with this performance, the octree has not been fully exploited. Elseberg et al. proposed an efficient octree for storing and compressing 3D data without loss of precision. Behley et al. proposed an index-based octree that improves radius neighbor search in three-dimensional data significantly, but it does not support KNN search and dynamic updates. When these static trees are used in real robotic applications, the entire tree has to be re-built from scratch again and again, and this is so time-consuming that the robots may fail to run.

- Our method: i-Octree
  - dynamic octree; incremental updates with new points; fast NNS
  - efficient in time and memory; adaptable to various point types; on-tree down-sampling; box-wise delete
  - experiments: randomized data + real-world open datasets
  - vs ikd-Tree (state-of-the-art incremental k-d tree): run-time -64% build, -66% insertion, -30% KNN, -56% radius search
  - LiDAR SLAM on real data: over twice the speed of original method, often higher accuracy
  - open-sourced on Github
- Paper organization
  - Section II: design of i-Octree
  - Section III: experiments
  - Section IV: conclusions

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Many robotic applications need nearest neighbors search (NNS), for example real-time LiDAR-based simultaneous localization and mapping (SLAM) and motion planning, where data is sampled sequentially and real-time mapping is essential. In LiDAR-based SLAM, NNS is crucial for computing features, estimating normals, and matching new points to the map. Recent advances in LiDAR technology have reduced the cost, size, weight, and power of LiDAR significantly, and also made LiDAR high performance, so it has become an essential sensor for robots. But this also makes NNS more challenging. A current LiDAR sensor can produce a large amount of 3D points per second, with centimeter accuracy at a measuring range of hundreds of meters. This large amount of sequential data has to be processed in real-time, which is quite challenging on robots that have limited onboard computing resources. So to make NNS efficient, it is very important to maintain a large map that supports highly efficient queries and dynamic updates with newly arriving points in real-time.

Various static tree data structures have been proposed, but they struggle to meet these demands. R-tree and R \ast -tree partition the data by grouping nearby points into their minimum bounding rectangle in the next higher level of the tree. k-d tree is a well-known instance of splitting the space. The octree splits the space recursively into eight equal axis-aligned cubes, and these form the volumes represented by eight child nodes. k-d tree is a favored data structure in general k-nearest neighbors (KNN) search libraries, but it is hard to draw a final conclusion on whether the k-d tree is better suited for NNS than other data structures. Comparative studies show that different implementations of k-d trees can perform very differently, and that the octree is among the best performing algorithms, especially for radius search, because it partitions the search space regularly. Even with this performance, the octree has not been fully exploited. Elseberg et al. proposed an efficient octree for storing and compressing 3D data without loss of precision. Behley et al. proposed an index-based octree that improves radius neighbor search in three-dimensional data significantly, but it does not support KNN search and dynamic updates. When these static trees are used in real robotic applications, the entire tree has to be re-built from scratch again and again, and this is so time-consuming that the robots may fail to run.

In this paper we propose a dynamic octree structure, called i-Octree, which updates the octree incrementally with new points and allows fast NNS. Our i-Octree is also very efficient in both time and memory, it can be adapted to various types of points, and it allows on-tree down-sampling and box-wise delete. We run validation experiments on randomized data and on real-world open datasets to assess how effective i-Octree is. In the randomized data experiments, i-Octree significantly improves runtime compared to the state-of-the-art incremental k-d tree, which is ikd-Tree that was proposed recently. It reduces run-time by 64% for building the tree, 66% for inserting points, 30% for KNN search, and 56% for radius neighbors search. Also, when we apply it to real-world data in LiDAR-based SLAM, i-Octree gives a big improvement in time performance. It is more than twice as fast as the original method and often has higher accuracy. Our implementation of i-Octree is open-sourced on Github.

The rest of the paper is organized as follows: Section II describes the design of i-Octree, Section III shows the experiments, and Section IV gives conclusions.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Nearest neighbors search (NNS) is necessary in many robotic applications, such as real-time LiDAR-based simultaneous localization and mapping (SLAM) and motion planning, where data is sampled sequentially and real-time mapping is essential. For example, in LiDAR-based SLAM, NNS is crucial to compute features [1,2], estimate normals [3,4], and match new points to the map [5,6,7,8]. Recent advances in LiDAR technology have not only significantly reduced the cost, size, weight, and power of LiDAR but also enabled its high performance, making it an essential sensor for robots [9]. However, this also poses challenges to NNS. Current LiDAR sensors can produce a large amount of 3D points per second with centimeter accuracy at a measuring range of hundreds of meters. This large amount of sequential data must be processed in real-time, which is quite challenging on robots with limited onboard computing resources. To guarantee efficient NNS, it is vital to maintain a large map that supports highly efficient queries and dynamic updates with newly arriving points in real-time.

Although various static tree data structures have been proposed, they struggle to meet these demands. R-tree [10] and R \ast -tree [11] partition the data by grouping nearby points into their minimum bounding rectangle in the next higher level of the tree. k-d tree [12] is a well-known instance of splitting the space. The octree recursively splits the space equally into eight axis-aligned cubes, which form the volumes represented by eight child nodes. Although k-d tree is a favored data structure in general k-nearest neighbors (KNN) search libraries, it is hard to draw any final conclusion as to whether the k-d tree is better suited for NNS than other data structures. Comparative studies [13,14] show that the performance of different k-d tree implementations can vary widely, and that the octree is amongst the best performing algorithms, especially for radius search, due to its regular partitioning of the search space. Despite this performance, the octree has not been fully exploited. Elseberg et al. [15] proposed an efficient octree to store and compress 3D data without loss of precision. Behley et al. [16] proposed an index-based octree that significantly improves radius neighbor search in three-dimensional data, but KNN search and dynamic updates are not enabled. When these static trees are incorporated in real robotic applications, repeatedly re-building the entire tree from scratch [17] is inevitable, which is so time-consuming that the robots may fail to run.

In this paper, we propose a dynamic octree structure called i-Octree, which incrementally updates the octree with new points and enables fast NNS. In addition, i-Octree is highly efficient in both time and memory, adaptable to various types of points, and allows on-tree down-sampling and box-wise delete. We conduct validation experiments on both randomized data and real-world open datasets to assess the effectiveness of i-Octree. In the randomized data experiments, i-Octree shows significant runtime improvements over the state-of-the-art incremental k-d tree (i.e., the recently proposed ikd-Tree [9]). Specifically, it reduces run-time by 64% for building the tree, 66% for point insertion, 30% for KNN search, and 56% for radius neighbors search. Moreover, when applied to real-world data in LiDAR-based SLAM, i-Octree shows remarkable time performance enhancements, achieving over twice the speed of the original method while often maintaining higher accuracy. Furthermore, our implementation of i-Octree is open-sourced on Github.

The rest of the paper is organized as follows: the design of i-Octree is described in Section II. Experiments are shown in Section III, followed by conclusions in Section IV.
